items.title: Territorial Acknowledgement
notes: Councillor Vasic opened the meeting with the following Territorial Acknowledgement:

We would like to begin by acknowledging that the land on which we are gathering from today is the land traditionally cared for by the Haudenosaunee, Anishnaabe and Neutral People. We also acknowledge the enduring presence and deep traditional knowledge and philosophies of the Indigenous People with whom we share this land today.

items.title: The ‘holiday season’ is language with a shared understanding of dominant
notes: cultures; it generally means the celebration of American Thanksgiving, Christmas, and New Year’s between November and January. If we change our perspective and acknowledge that there are additional holidays celebrated by friends, colleagues, and neighbours during that period, we arrive at the recognition of a season of many holidays.
Alongside Christmas and New Year’s in Canada, which are steeped in meaningful personal traditions of gatherings, food, and sentiment for those that celebrate, are equally significant celebrations:
• Diwali was celebrated on November 12
• Hanukkah occurs from December 7 to 15
• Bodhi Day, a Buddhist celebration, is December 8, 2023 • Winter Solstice is December 21
• Dongzhi Festival, celebrated in Japan, China and Taiwan is from December 21 to 23
• Christmas is December 25
• Kwanzaa is from December 26 to January 1
• New Year’s Day is January 1
• Orthodox Christmas is January 7
• Maghi, a Sikh observance, will take place on January 13 • Lohri, the Punjab Winter Festival, is January 13
• Haudenosaunee Mid-winter Ceremonies will be celebrated during the new moon in January and lasts for approximately eight days • Lunar New Year will take place on February 10
• Vasant Panchami, a Hindu observance, is February 14

• Magha, a Buddhist observance, will take place on February 24 Despite the notable differences such as religion, date and appeal, together these holidays remind us of human desires to be connected to each other.

For many years, traditional Christmas decorations have been put up in municipal facilities and spaces across Waterloo. This décor is intended to recognize the joy of the holiday season with the community. To create a more inclusive and welcoming environment, banners recognizing the season of many celebrations will be displayed in City of Waterloo facilities until February.

items.title: During the 16 Days of Activism, Canadians reflect on the presence of
notes: gender based violence in our own country. On December 6, many in our community and across Canada will pause to remember the 14 young women murdered at Polytechnique Montreal and all women who have suffered gender-based violence.

These days of remembrance and activism push us to consider the links between sexism, transphobia and homophobia, and the greater risks faced by women, trans people, non-binary people and gender-diverse people.
The additional impact of racism and colonialism put Indigenous women, girls and Two Spirit people at even greater risk, similarly the impact of ableism on women with disabilities.

As a City, we recognize the importance of taking action on the devastating impacts of gender-based violence. We are also mindful that challenging sexist and transphobic systems must not be limited to a few observances throughout the year but an ongoing action.
At the beginning of this Council meeting, we pause to think about the needs of our community. May we show wisdom and compassion in all our decisions.

items.title: Urban Forest Management Strategy
notes: Introduction
Report No.: COM2023-037
Prepared By: Derek Brick

Derek Brick introduced the report and the consultant, and noted there were changes in some of the numbers since the report was published, including that the current tree canopy was 32.5% rather than the reported 15%, and that the current funding gap is $400,000 rather than the reported $7.5 million.

John McNeil, Managing Partner, McNeil Urban Forestry Inc. gave a presentation outlining the Urban Forest Management Strategy, highlighting the link to the new strategic plan and the benefits to citizens. They then responded to questions of Council.
Robin Milne and Derek Brick also responded to questions of Council.

items.title: Boulevard Gardens
notes: Report No.: IPPW2023-049
Prepared By: Ainsley Rego and Grant Curlew

Masha Kuznetsova, Resident of Waterloo gave a presentation asking the City to consider making further changes to the Lot Maintenance By-law, which include increasing the grass height, removing the Buffer Strip around naturalized areas, and encouraging homeowners to transition to natural lawns. They then responded to questions of Council.
Grant Curlew, Ainsley Rego, Jenny Renaud, Nicole Papke, Derek Brick, Mark Dykstra, Robin Milne and Francis Reyes also responded to questions of Council.

items.title: New Business
notes: Councillor Hanmer wanted to shout out the facilities staff at RIM Park and Albert McCormick Community Centre for their hard work during the USA Canada Cup, run by the Waterloo Girls Hockey Association. There were 78 Under 22 and Under 18 AA female hockey teams from all over Canada and USA, and over 100 scouts from NCAA Universities, Canadian Universities, and Hockey Canada. She offered a special shout out to the paramedics and fire team.

Councillor Roe wanted to mention that last Thursday, November 30, she, Mayor McCabe and Councillor Roach met with YMCA of Three Rivers Immigration Services, and they brought newcomers to Canada into Council Chambers to explain municipal government, explain the two-tier system, and answer questions.

Councillor Freeman wanted to shout out the Professional Fire Fighters Association who stood in the rain on December 3rd during the Lights of Love by Hospice Waterloo Region, where hundreds of people gathered to remember loved ones who had passed.

Councillor Wright mentioned the tree lighting at Waterloo Public Square on Friday, December 1st, with a shout out to the BIA and City staff for their support. She also offered her thanks to the Dunn Family for donating the tree.
Mayor McCabe wanted to thank all the vendors that came out to the Holiday Pop-up Market held on December 1st and 2nd in the Waterloo Public Square.
Mayor McCabe also thanked the staff for helping to organize the disability seminars at the Waterloo Main Library.

motions.item_title: Mayor McCabe – Protection of Waterloo’s Natural Heritage Areas and
motions.text: WHEREAS in November 2022, the Government of Ontario passed Bill 23, More Homes Built Faster Act, as part of Ontario's Housing Supply Action Plan with the goal of building 1.5 million new homes in Ontario by 2031, and WHEREAS Bill 23 mandates that, upon legislative proclamation, all land use planning be transitioned from regional governments – the Region of Waterloo – to local municipalities such as the City of Waterloo, and WHEREAS Waterloo City Council has and continues to value and take measures to conserve significant natural features and systems through adoption of environmental policies and municipal decision-making, and understands the importance of conserving significant green spaces in a natural state and to minimize disturbances to such spaces, and WHEREAS Waterloo City Council’s Official Plan, Strategic Plan and Economic Development Strategy outline a long term commitment to building a community that is vibrant, diverse and sustainable as the city continues to intensify and urbanize, and WHEREAS Waterloo City Council acknowledges and understands the importance of rural communities and their contributions particularly with food security, preservation of sensitive natural heritage areas/systems and other green spaces, and economic development, and WHEREAS Waterloo City Council understands and appreciates that the Countryside Line is a boundary that protects the cultural, economic, and environmental heritage of our neighbouring municipalities’ rural lands from the pressures of urban sprawl and that the Countryside Line protects the integrity of rural communities from suburban expansion, and WHEREAS the City of Waterloo has, for decades, actively planned to grow inward through a comprehensive growth management (intensification) strategy, and accordingly has sufficient land currently and until 2050 to accommodate the growing population within Waterloo’s existing municipal boundaries, and WHEREAS past and present Waterloo City Councils have been leaders in environmental protection and understand that it is our responsibility to protect our environment, and that sound urban planning helps protect the environment while enabling the city to grow, THEREFORE be it resolved that Waterloo City Council reaffirm its longstanding practice of acquiring and protecting sensitive natural heritage areas/systems and green spaces from development, and managing growth in a sustainable manner.
